name: Kanite
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Young, Rosemary. 1962. The phonemes of Kanite, Kamano, Benabena, and Gahuku. Oceania Linguistic Monographs; also Gibson & McCarthy 2003 Kanite grammar sketch (SIL, 403).

new_statements.quote: In these four languages the contrastive supra-segmental feature is not so much one of pitch levels or stress intensity as of syllable emphasis. That is, each language has one distinct supra-segmental phoneme which when it occurs gives contrast to affected syllables over neutral syllables. In KANITE and GAHUKU it is a phoneme of tone, which has been described as high tone and which contrasts with syllables which may be described as being either low tone or toneless. Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed. ... KANITE ke'na "skirt" 'ke'na "bamboo" ... [p.99] In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable.
new_statements.citation: Young, Rosemary. 1962. The phonemes of Kanite, Kamano, Benabena, and Gahuku. In James C. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kanite has no positionally fixed word stress: the single contrastive suprasegmental is a lexically placed high tone (vs low/toneless syllables), with minimal pairs differing only in which syllable carries it; stress (intensity) always falls on the high-toned syllable(s). Every word has at least one high tone; a noun's tone is perturbed by a preceding adjective (conditioned by adjective class and the noun's initial-syllable vowel). The later SIL Organised Phonology Data (Gibson & McCarthy, 1992/2004, p.3) restates: 'Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.'; McCarthy 1965 fn.: 'Stress is phonemic but carries a low functional load.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Kanite (words may carry more than one high tone, e.g. tʌ'ʔe'ne 'our teeth'); Young describes secondary/second stress only for Kamano and Benabena.
new_statements.exceptions: No toneless words except nouns bound into compound verb expressions; noun tone perturbed (sandhi) after adjectives; no perturbation between adjacent nouns and verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic description based on isolated words and minimal pairs; tone sandhi noted at the adjective+noun phrase level. OPD describes the Kemeyu Kanite variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Young 1962 describes Kanite proper (fieldwork by Gibson & McCarthy from 1957 in a Kanite village); the 1992/2004 OPD is headed 'Kanite (Kemeyu Kanite)', villages Kemeyu, Anupalu, Ko'kopi, Kuana (Okapa district). The grammar sketch also carries notes on Inoke (= Inoke-Yate, ISO ino, glottocode inok1238, a separate Glottolog language) and the Kagufi sub-dialect; the stress/tone statements quoted do not concern those.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 (pp. 98-99): the one contrastive suprasegmental in Kanite is a tone phoneme (high vs low/toneless), lexically placed with minimal pairs (ke'na 'skirt' vs 'ke'na 'bamboo'); tone occurs on nouns and verbs, no toneless words; noun tone perturbed by preceding adjective; 'In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable.'
